prompt:
A team is considering a weekly meeting, but its members already feel overloaded. Explain how to decide whether a meeting is the right tool. A response of around 120 words is enough.

Write the requested response as one self-contained paragraph of plain text. Do not use a title, headings, bullet points, numbered lists, Markdown formatting, code fences, or line breaks. Include only the requested content, without any introductory or closing commentary from the assistant. Keep the approximate word target given in the task. If the task calls for an email, dialogue, steps, or calculations, express that content within the same paragraph.
base_prompt: A team is considering a weekly meeting, but its members already feel overloaded. Explain how to decide whether a meeting is the right tool. A response of around 120 words is enough.
text: Start by defining the specific problem the weekly meeting would solve: a decision that needs joint discussion, a dependency that repeatedly causes delays, or information that cannot be conveyed clearly in writing. If the purpose is status reporting, announcements, or routine updates, use an asynchronous channel such as a shared dashboard, brief written update, or project board instead. Estimate the cost honestly by multiplying meeting length by attendees, preparation time, and context switching, then compare it with the expected benefit. A meeting is justified when real-time conversation will materially improve decisions, coordination, or relationships. If one is needed, invite only essential participants, set a clear agenda and decision owner, keep it short, and review after several weeks whether it still earns its place.
